tasks.locator: Abstract; Methods › Study Design and Procedure, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Results, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: 17 healthy adults (9 men, 8 women; mean age 27.3) who had not used cannabis for at least 30 days (mean 398 days, median 365, range 30 to 1,825 since last use) each completed six 8.5-hour sessions at least a week apart: flower with 0, 10 or 25 mg THC loaded, smoked in a small handheld pipe or vaporized in a desktop vaporizer and inhaled from a balloon, over 10 minutes. Method order was counterbalanced across people and dose order randomized within each method.

tasks.locator: Methods › Study Drug
tasks.extracted: Flower from the US National Institute on Drug Abuse supply with 13.4% delta-9-THC (placebo batch under 0.01%); the same weight of plant material (186.6 mg) in every session, with placebo material mixed in to reach 10 mg. The 'dose' is the THC in the material loaded; how much THC left each device was not measured.

tasks.locator: Table (Drug effect row); Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Abstract
tasks.extracted: Drug-effect rating (0 to 100), mean (SD) peak change: smoked 45.7 (26.4) at 10 mg and 66.4 (28.6) at 25 mg; vaporized 69.5 (26.4) and 77.5 (23.4); placebo sessions 11.2 (15.9) and 2.1 (5.2). Vaporized exceeded smoked at 10 mg (flagged P below .05) and no difference was flagged at 25 mg. Editors' calculation (unpaired, conservative): vaporized minus smoked 23.8 points (95% CI 5.4 to 42.2) at 10 mg and 11.1 (-7.2 to 29.4) at 25 mg.

tasks.locator: Results › Whole-Blood THC Concentrations, 1st paragraph; Abstract
tasks.extracted: Peak whole-blood THC, mean (SD) ng/mL: vaporized 7.5 (5.5) at 10 mg and 14.4 (9.4) at 25 mg; smoked 3.8 (5.9) and 10.2 (12.4). Peak at the first sample (10 minutes), back to zero within 4 hours in every condition. The paper reports no test or interval for the difference between methods. Editors' calculation (unpaired): difference 3.7 ng/mL (-0.3 to 7.7) at 10 mg and 4.2 (-3.5 to 11.9) at 25 mg.

tasks.locator: Table (Physiological measures); Results › Physiological Measures, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Heart rate, mean (SD) peak rise in beats per minute: smoked 11.3 (10.4) at 10 mg and 19.1 (17.1) at 25 mg; vaporized 23.3 (11.8) and 26.8 (16.6); placebo sessions -3.7 and -4.3. Only the 10 mg difference between methods was flagged (P below .05); editors' calculation (unpaired): 12.0 beats per minute (4.2 to 19.8) at 10 mg and 7.7 (-4.1 to 19.5) at 25 mg. Peak at the first measurement (10 minutes); back to baseline within 3 hours.

tasks.locator: Table (Cognitive measures); Results › Cognitive and Psychomotor Measures, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Task performance, peak change from baseline. Digit Symbol Substitution (number correct): vaporized -8.3 at 10 mg and -13.8 at 25 mg, both below placebo; smoked +3.4 and -7.0, neither different from its placebo session. Differences between methods were flagged for three contrasts only: Divided Attention distance at 10 mg, and Digit Symbol Substitution attempted and correct at 25 mg. Deficits typically peaked 30 to 60 minutes after dosing and in some instances had not returned to baseline at 6 to 8 hours.

tasks.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table
tasks.extracted: At 25 mg both methods raised ratings of unpleasant effects (smoked 32.9, vaporized 24.4), anxious or nervous (21.4; 25.5), memory impairment (14.2; 16.2), throat irritation or coughing (27.8; 22.18) and difficulty performing routine tasks (30.6; 34.2) over placebo, with no difference between methods flagged for the unpleasant, anxious, memory or throat items. Paranoid ratings rose over placebo only after vaporized 25 mg; sick only after smoked 25 mg. Between-method differences were flagged for 4 of 20 rating items at 10 mg and 2 at 25 mg.

tasks.locator: Results › Adverse Events
tasks.extracted: Adverse events as reported: two people vomited (one after 25 mg vaporized, one after 25 mg smoked) and one had hallucinations after 25 mg vaporized. No counts are given for placebo or 10 mg sessions and no other events are listed; the abstract's statement of increased incidence at 25 mg rests on these three events.

tasks.locator: Results › Subjective Drug Effects, 2nd paragraph; Results › Correlations Between Whole-Blood THC Concentrations and Pharmacodynamic Profiles; Discussion, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: After both 25 mg conditions mean drug-effect ratings were still above baseline at 6 hours (smoked 12.2, vaporized 10.8) although blood THC was back to zero within 4 hours. Blood THC correlated with drug-effect ratings (r above 0.37) and heart rate (r above 0.24) but, for performance, only with Digit Symbol Substitution correct at 25 mg vaporized (r = -0.32); the authors conclude that blood THC is not a valid indicator of intoxication or impairment.

tasks.locator: Introduction, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors state that earlier controlled comparisons (not read here) found similar profiles for smoked and vaporized cannabis, and suggest that the different result here may be because those studies let people adjust their dose while this one gave a fixed amount, and that vaporizing delivers THC more efficiently because smoking loses THC to combustion and side-stream smoke (not tested).

tasks.locator: Limitations, 1st paragraph; Discussion, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: a limited range of doses, one type of cannabis (raw plant material, high THC, low cannabidiol), one vaporizer at a fixed temperature, enrolment limited to people who rarely use cannabis, and a sample too small to study individual characteristics. They note that the largest amount given (0.19 g of 13.4% THC flower) is smaller and weaker than prerolls sold in dispensaries (about 1 g, often over 18% THC, citing a 2018 survey that was not read here).

tasks.locator: Study Registration Dates; Study Overview; Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures; Design Details
tasks.extracted: Registry record NCT03676166: study start 16 June 2016, completion 17 January 2017, first submitted 16 September 2018 (after the study ended); actual enrolment 18 against 17 analysed in the paper; registered primary outcome quantity of THC in blood at 8 hours; secondary outcomes drug-effect rating, Digit Symbol Substitution, Paced Auditory Serial Addition and Divided Attention.

tasks.locator: Methods › Statistical Analysis; Methods › Study Design and Procedure, 1st paragraph; Table (all rows)
tasks.extracted: The Table reports 32 outcomes (editors' count). Contrasts against placebo within each method used a threshold of P below .025 (Bonferroni for two comparisons); the contrasts between methods at each amount were treated as orthogonal and tested at P below .05 with no correction; nothing was corrected across the 32 outcomes (up to 192 planned contrasts, editors' count), and no interval or exact P value is given for any contrast. No double-dummy procedure was used to hide the inhalation method from participants and staff. The sample size of 17 was justified by a meta-analysis of six acute drug administration studies (reference 24), not by a cannabis route comparison.

tasks.locator: Article notes (Conflict of Interest Disclosures; Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor)
tasks.extracted: Funding as printed: the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration (SAMHSA, a US federal agency), which also provided technical assistance on design and conduct, analysis and interpretation, and preparation, review and approval of the manuscript and the decision to submit it; it had no role in collecting or managing study data. Disclosures as printed: Dr Vandrey reports personal fees, consulting or honoraria from Zynerba Pharmaceuticals, Insys Therapeutics, Battelle Memorial Institute and Canopy Health Innovations Inc outside the submitted work; Drs Vandrey, Spindle and Mitchell report SAMHSA grants during the study; Dr Cone reports consulting for ConeChem Research and RTI during the study; Dr Schlienz reports National Institute on Drug Abuse grants outside the work; Dr Hayes reports funding from the Department of Health and Human Services, SAMHSA, the National Laboratory Certification Program and RTI International.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Methods › Analytic Sample, 1st paragraph; Results, 1st paragraph; Table 1
tasks.extracted: 2,553 young adults (mean age 19.3; 57.9% women; 47.3% Hispanic) from a Southern California school-based cohort answered one survey between June 2018 and October 2019, a year after high-school graduation (75% participation). Outcome data were available for 2,194 (bronchitic symptoms), 2,396 (wheeze) and 2,389 (shortness of breath). Bronchitic symptoms were daily cough for 3 months in a row, congestion or phlegm other than with a cold, and/or bronchitis in the previous 12 months; wheeze in the previous 12 months; shortness of breath when hurrying on level ground or walking up a slight hill.

tasks.locator: Results › Respiratory Health Outcomes and Levels of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Table 1; Table 2 footnote f
tasks.extracted: Of 2,443 people with cannabis vaping data, 939 (38.4%) reported ever vaping THC or hash oil or dabs (concentrated cannabis): 204 only in their lifetime, 490 in the past 6 months but not the past 30 days, 90 on 1 or 2 days and 155 on 3 or more days in the past 30; 110 people had no cannabis vaping data. 1,095 of 2,553 (42.9%) reported ever vaping nicotine. Smoked cannabis on 3 or more days in the past 30: 20.3%; cigarettes: 3.8%.

tasks.locator: Results › Respiratory Health Outcomes and Levels of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping, 1st paragraph; Table 2 (total row and cannabis vaping rows)
tasks.extracted: Overall 384 of 2,194 (17.5%) reported bronchitic symptoms, 312 of 2,396 (13.0%) wheeze and 488 of 2,389 (20.4%) shortness of breath. Among the 384 with bronchitic symptoms, 185 (48.2%) had never vaped cannabis; Table 2's percentages are shares of people with each outcome, not rates within each vaping group, so the paper gives no symptom rate by vaping group.

tasks.locator: Table 2 (cannabis vaping rows, bronchitic symptoms column; group sizes in the No./Total column; footnotes b and f)
tasks.extracted: Editors' rough calculation from Table 2 counts, not in the paper (Table 2 gives cases by vaping group and group sizes out of 2,553 but no rates within groups). Bronchitic symptoms among people who never vaped cannabis: 185 of 1,504 (12.3%) if everyone without symptom data is counted as symptom-free, or about 14% (185 of about 1,293) if the 359 people with missing symptom data are spread evenly across groups (86% of each group having data). Vaping on 1 or 2 days in the past 30: 24 of 90 (26.7%) or about 31% (24 of about 77). Vaping on 3 or more days: 36 of 155 (23.2%) or about 27% (36 of about 133). The paper says people who gave no respiratory data were less likely to report never vaping nicotine and smoking cigarettes (supplement table, not read), so even spreading may not hold.

tasks.locator: Table 3 (bronchitic symptoms columns, frequency of vaping cannabis rows); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Bronchitic symptoms and cannabis vaping, full model (adjusted for nicotine vaping, cigarette smoking, smoked cannabis, age, sex, race and ethnicity, financial status, body mass index), adjusted odds ratios against never vaping cannabis: lifetime but not past 6 months 1.73 (95% CI 1.01 to 2.96); past 6 months but not past 30 days 1.63 (1.04 to 2.56); 1 or 2 days in the past 30 2.79 (1.42 to 5.47); 3 or more days 2.19 (1.18 to 4.06). Sociodemographic model only: 1.47 (0.97 to 2.23), 1.44 (1.07 to 1.94), 2.95 (1.75 to 4.98), 2.51 (1.63 to 3.84). The abstract prints different values for the full model; Table 3 is used.

tasks.locator: Table 3 (wheeze columns); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Wheeze and cannabis vaping, full model: 3 or more days in the past 30 2.27 (1.17 to 4.37); other levels not reliably raised (1.12, 0.61 to 2.03; 1.47, 0.92 to 2.35; 1.84, 0.88 to 3.86). Sociodemographic model: 2.13 (1.35 to 3.36) in the top band and 1.47 (1.08 to 2.00) for past 6 months but not past 30 days.

tasks.locator: Table 3 (shortness of breath columns); Results › Associations of Nicotine and Cannabis Vaping With Respiratory Health Symptoms, 4th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Shortness of breath and cannabis vaping: sociodemographic model raised at 3 or more days (1.67, 1.09 to 2.53) and past 6 months only (1.35, 1.04 to 1.75); in the full model no level was reliably raised (0.90, 0.57 to 1.40; 1.25, 0.86 to 1.84; 1.55, 0.81 to 2.96; 3 or more days 1.41, 0.80 to 2.48).

tasks.locator: Table 3 (frequency of vaping nicotine rows); Discussion, 1st and 2nd paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Nicotine vaping on 3 or more days in the past 30, sociodemographic model: bronchitic symptoms 1.78 (1.32 to 2.41), wheeze 1.41 (1.01 to 1.96), shortness of breath 1.45 (1.08 to 1.96); full model 0.96 (0.63 to 1.46), 0.85 (0.54 to 1.35), 0.96 (0.64 to 1.42), with no nicotine vaping level reliably associated with any outcome. The authors say residual confounding by cannabis vaping and by smoking cigarettes or cannabis could partly explain the earlier associations.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Limitations, 1st paragraph
tasks.extracted: Limits and explanations given by the authors: cross-sectional design, so temporality is unknown; a school-based Southern California sample with 75% participation, not nationally representative; the cannabis vaping measure includes dabs; longitudinal research on cannabis vaping and symptoms is lacking; possible reasons for a difference from nicotine vaping (chemicals in THC e-liquids, device and heating differences, tampering with products, deeper or longer puffs) were not measured.

tasks.locator: Table 3 (cannabis vaping rows, bronchitic symptoms, full adjustment); Methods › Measures
tasks.extracted: Editors' reading of Table 3: odds of bronchitic symptoms were raised even in people whose last cannabis vaping was more than 6 months before the survey (1.73, 1.01 to 2.96), against 2.19 to 2.79 for vaping on days in the past 30, so the data show no clear gradient with recency; this argues for caution about an effect of recent vaping and for residual confounding. No product, device, source, additive or amount was recorded, and tobacco in joints or blunts was not recorded.

tasks.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title
tasks.extracted: Weekly hospital admissions for the national vaping lung injury outbreak (EVALI) peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019, within the period (June 2018 to October 2019) in which this survey was taken; the survey did not record which products people vaped or whether anyone had that injury.

tasks.locator: Article notes (Conflict of Interest Disclosures; Funding/Support; Role of the Funder/Sponsor)
tasks.extracted: Funding as printed: National Cancer Institute grants U54CA180905, R01CA229617-01 and K24DA048160; the funders had no role in design, conduct, analysis, interpretation, writing or the decision to submit; no conflicts reported.

tasks.locator: Methods › Case Definitions; Table 1 (Case Definitions for Patients with EVALI)
tasks.extracted: CDC case definitions as printed in the paper: confirmed and probable cases both need vaping or dabbing in the 90 days before symptom onset, a lung infiltrate on chest imaging and no evidence in the medical record of an alternative plausible diagnosis; confirmed cases also need negative respiratory viral, influenza and other clinically indicated infection tests; probable cases may have an infection identified, or incomplete testing, when the clinical team judges the infection is not the sole cause of the lung injury. State and local health departments assigned case status.

tasks.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Case status row)
tasks.extracted: As of 14 January 2020, all 50 states, the District of Columbia, the US Virgin Islands and Puerto Rico had reported 2,668 hospitalized EVALI patients to CDC: 1,401 (53%) confirmed and 1,267 (47%) probable cases.

tasks.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Sex, Median age, Age group, Race/Ethnicity rows)
tasks.extracted: Median age 24 years (range 13 to 85); 404 (15%) aged 13 to 17, 979 (37%) 18 to 24, 631 (24%) 25 to 34, 335 (13%) 35 to 44, 223 (9%) 45 to 64, 47 (2%) 65 and over, of 2,619 with age; 1,731 of 2,606 (66%) male; of 1,856 with race and ethnicity, 73% non-Hispanic white and 15% Hispanic.

tasks.locator: Abstract; main text before the Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Table (Substances used rows and footnotes)
tasks.extracted: Among 2,022 patients with information on substances used (76% of 2,668), who had vaped or dabbed at least one substance in the 3 months before symptom onset: any THC-containing product 1,650 (82%); any nicotine-containing product 1,162 (57%); both 834 (41%); THC only 669 (33%); nicotine only 274 (14%); neither 44 (2%). Product information was missing for 24% of patients. The four exclusive categories add to 1,821, not 2,022.

tasks.locator: Main text before the Discussion, 3rd paragraph; Figure 1 title
tasks.extracted: Weekly hospital admissions for EVALI peaked at 215 in the week of 15 September 2019 and have declined steadily since.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 4th and 5th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Limits given by the authors: product-use data missing for 24% of patients and many not interviewed; the emergency visit query may have been affected by awareness of the outbreak; coverage of the surveillance system uneven and changing over time. The report covers hospitalized patients only and does not report deaths or what happened to patients after discharge (it says long-term consequences need long-term follow-up).

tasks.locator: Discussion, 2nd paragraph; Discussion, 4th paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors state that vitamin E acetate is strongly linked to THC-containing products used by EVALI patients (citing the lung-fluid study), that a minority of patients consistently report only nicotine-containing products (possible reasons: patients may not report or know the content of what they vaped; the high sensitivity of the case definition likely lowered specificity, so some patients may not have EVALI; or the reports may be accurate), and that evidence is not sufficient to rule out other chemicals of concern, in THC- or non-THC-containing products, in some cases. It is not known whether additives other than vitamin E acetate could cause similar injury.
tasks.quote: evidence is not sufficient to rule out the contribution of other chemicals of concern

tasks.locator: Abstract; Results, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Lung-lavage (BAL) fluid from 51 patients with EVALI in 16 states (collected August to December 2019 during routine clinical care; 25 confirmed, 26 probable; median age 23, 69% male) and from 99 healthy participants of an unrelated Ohio State University tobacco-product study (52 who neither vaped nor smoked, 18 who vaped nicotine only, 29 who smoked cigarettes only; sampled 2016 to 2019, 90 before 2019). The authors call the cases a convenience sample; collection was not standardized. New York is not among the 16 states.

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3 (vitamin E acetate row)
tasks.extracted: Vitamin E acetate was found in lung fluid from 48 of 51 patients (94%) and from none of the 99 healthy participants (0 of 52, 0 of 18, 0 of 29). Editors' calculation, exact binomial 95% intervals: patients 83.8% to 98.8%; comparators 0% to 3.7%.

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 3; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Other priority substances in patients' lung fluid: coconut oil 1 of 48, limonene 1 of 39 (the limonene patient had no vitamin E acetate or THC and reported daily flavoured nicotine products); medium-chain triglyceride oil 0 of 49, plant oil 0 of 49, squalane 0 of 38, squalene 0 of 38, pinenes and 3-carene 0 of 39, petroleum distillates 0 of 12. None of these was found in any comparator.

tasks.locator: Results, 4th paragraph; Table 4; Discussion, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: The three patients without detectable vitamin E acetate were all probable cases, with other plausible diagnoses recorded in Table 4, so all 25 confirmed cases were positive (editors' deduction; exact binomial 95% interval for 25 of 25, 86.3% to 100%, editors' calculation).

tasks.locator: Abstract; Results, 2nd and 4th paragraphs; Table 2
tasks.extracted: THC or its metabolites were found in lung fluid from 40 of 47 patients (85%); 9 of 11 patients who reported no THC product use in the 90 days before illness had THC or metabolites in lung fluid; nicotine or metabolites in 30 of 47 (64%). Self-reported (43 patients): nicotine products only 7 (16%), THC products only 11 (26%), both 22 (51%).

tasks.locator: Results, 3rd paragraph; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Healthy comparators: none reported vaping THC products; urine THC biomarkers positive in 21 of 82 (26%); nicotine or metabolites in 52% of lung fluids; all negative for every priority substance.

tasks.locator: Introduction, 1st and 2nd paragraphs; Discussion, 5th and 6th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Second-hand context quoted by the authors from a CDC web page and an earlier CDC report (none read here): more than 2,400 hospitalized patients and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019; 78% under 35; nearly half (47%) needed intensive care for respiratory failure. FDA testing found vitamin E acetate in 49% of case-associated THC product samples and none of 197 case-associated nicotine products; in Minnesota 0 of 10 products seized in 2018 contained it against 20 of 20 THC products seized in September 2019.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 8th and 9th paragraphs; Discussion, 7th paragraph
tasks.extracted: Limits stated by the authors: vitamin E acetate may be a marker of another toxicant; products formed when it is heated were not examined; sample collection was not standardized; timing and burden of exposure could not be assessed; case and comparator samples come from independent studies at single time points, so unknown confounding remains. Animal studies are needed to show whether vitamin E acetate alone causes the injury.

tasks.locator: Acknowledgments; Footnotes
tasks.extracted: Funding as printed: National Cancer Institute grant P50CA180908; FDA Center for Tobacco Products grant P30CA016058; Ohio State University Pelotonia Intramural Research. Authors are mostly CDC staff, with Ohio State University and FDA authors; the publisher's disclosure forms were not read.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Introduction, 3rd and 4th paragraphs; Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1
tasks.extracted: Thirty-eight samples of fluid from vaporizer cartridges recovered from the first 10 New York State patients with EVALI for whom cartridges were obtained; two held nicotine and no cannabinoids and 36 held cannabinoids. The laboratory began receiving cartridges in August 2019.

tasks.locator: Results 3.2, 3rd paragraph; Table 1 (VEA column); Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Vitamin E acetate was found in 23 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids (64%), at 16 to 57% by mass (Table 1 maximum 57.6%; 58% in the Discussion); 13 held none above 1% by mass. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 46% to 79%, treating the 36 fluids as independent, which they are not.

tasks.locator: Results 3.2, 4th paragraph; Table 1 (MCT column)
tasks.extracted: Medium-chain triglyceride (MCT) oil, another diluent, was estimated at 3 to 24% by mass in the 15 fluids the text says held it (Table 1 marks 14, by the editors' count); 12 of the 13 fluids without vitamin E acetate held MCT oil and 2 held both. MCT was estimated roughly because standards for its components are not available.

tasks.locator: Results 3.1, 5th paragraph; Results 3.3; Table 2; Discussion 4.1, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Pesticides: myclobutanil was quantified in 22 fluids (up to 28.3 micrograms per gram), the pesticide synergist piperonyl butoxide in 18 (up to 24.1), and several other fungicides, insecticides and acaricides above 1 microgram per gram in 26; 31 of the 36 cannabinoid-containing fluids held at least one (editors' count). The authors judge the pattern intermittent and say EVALI is not due to a single pesticide. No mycotoxins (below 4.8 ng/g) and no synthetic cannabinoids or opioids (below 0.05% by mass) in any fluid.

tasks.locator: Results 3.4; Table 3; Discussion 4.2, 3rd paragraph
tasks.extracted: Of six commercial products bought online as cannabis-oil diluents or thickeners, two diluents and one thickener were essentially pure vitamin E acetate; the others were squalane-based or alpha-bisabolol-based. The sellers did not list ingredients on label or website.

tasks.locator: Conclusions
tasks.extracted: Update to 12 December 2019, given in the Conclusions without methods or a table: 206 fluids from 61 New York cases, 147 with THC and 59 with nicotine; 101 of the 147 THC-containing fluids (69%) held vitamin E acetate. Editors' calculation: exact 95% interval 61% to 76%, treating fluids as independent. Whether the first 38 fluids are included is not stated. The authors also cite CDC counts of 2,409 hospitalized cases and 52 deaths as of 12 December 2019, and 205 New York cases including 2 deaths as of 10 December.

tasks.locator: Abstract; Methods 2.1; Discussion 4.1, 2nd paragraph; Discussion 4.3, 2nd and 3rd paragraphs; Conclusions
tasks.extracted: Limits and inferences stated by the authors: the cause or causes of EVALI are unknown; extensive in vitro and in vivo studies are required to establish a causative role of vitamin E acetate or other agents. The paper has no cartridges from people who vaped without injury, gives no per-patient results, and does not say how the cartridges were judged illicit; its contrast with the laboratory's medical-program products is stated without data.

tasks.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations
tasks.extracted: Funding as printed: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors work at the New York State Department of Health (Wadsworth Center; Center for Environmental Health), the University at Albany and Albany Medical Center.

tasks.locator: Results 3.1, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 1
tasks.extracted: A library-matched GC-MS screen of liquid from 38 counterfeit or patient-provided THC cartridges, 4 CBD cartridges and medical-grade cartridges found more than 500 chemicals. Chemicals described as specific to the counterfeit or patient-provided cartridges include silicon compounds (siloxanes, tetramethyl silicate), esters, benzophenone, glycerol tricaprylate, terpenes and vitamin E acetate; Table 1 lists 47 entries for these cartridges against 13 for CBD and 15 for medical-grade (editors' count). No count of cartridges containing any compound is given.

tasks.locator: Methods 2.4 and 2.5; Results 3.2 and 3.3; Table 2
tasks.extracted: Aerosol from counterfeit cartridges, collected in one-litre bottles and sent to a commercial laboratory, held over 50 listed volatile compounds (Table 2 has 53 entries), seven of them on the FDA list of tobacco-smoke constituents; silicon, copper, nickel and lead were the most abundant elements in the liquid, up to 600 parts per million. Vapor-phase and metals results are shown for counterfeit cartridges only.

tasks.locator: Results 3.1, 3rd paragraph; Discussion, 6th paragraph
tasks.extracted: The authors say they found vitamin E acetate in many EVALI-associated liquids but not all, and that the other cartridges patients used earlier may have held it; medical-grade cartridges (number not stated; one is described as the reference) held retinol (vitamin A) acetate rather than vitamin E acetate and fewer contaminants than counterfeit cartridges, though some harmful chemicals were still identified in them.

tasks.locator: Discussion, 10th and 12th paragraphs
tasks.extracted: Conclusion as written: numerous respiratory toxicants in liquid and vapor phases were not present in medical or CBD products; a combination of hydrocarbons, oils, other toxic compounds and metals may contribute to EVALI together with vitamin E acetate rather than a single agent. The study is a laboratory screen with library-matched identifications, small comparison groups and no per-cartridge counts; the paper is not a review.

tasks.locator: Funding; Conflicts of Interest; author affiliations
tasks.extracted: Funding as printed: none external. Declared conflicts: none. Authors work at the University of Rochester Medical Center, The College at Brockport, the New York State Department of Health Center for Environmental Health and the University at Buffalo.
